claims.text: Phase stability in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys is primarily governed by the interplay of lattice distortions from atomic-size mismatch and electronic interactions.
Lattice distortions and electronic interactions cooperatively stabilize a dual FCC/BCC microstructure.
Small changes in Al content shift the balance between FCC and BCC phase fractions.
The FCC/BCC phase balance governs defect energetics and mechanical properties.
A mixed FCC/BCC Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni baseline composition can provide balanced high-temperature strength and cryogenic toughness.
Changing Al concentration by approximately ±5 at.% modulates local lattice distortion and electronic effects.
Lattice-distortion magnitude and FCC/BCC phase fractions mediate phase stability and the resulting combination of properties.
Atomic-size mismatch associated particularly with Al creates controlled local lattice distortions.
A stabilized dual-phase microstructure resists grain-boundary sliding at high temperatures.
A stabilized dual-phase microstructure suppresses the growth of irradiation-induced defects.
A stabilized dual-phase microstructure accommodates deformation at cryogenic temperatures.
Increasing Al slightly above the baseline will increase the BCC phase fraction while retaining a minor FCC phase.
The Al-induced increase in BCC fraction will enhance high-temperature strength.
The Al-induced increase in BCC fraction will enhance radiation tolerance through stabilized dislocation motion and defect trapping.
Slightly increasing Al will preserve cryogenic toughness despite increasing the BCC fraction.
Reducing Al below the baseline will increase the FCC phase fraction.
Reducing Al will potentially lower high-temperature strength and radiation tolerance.
Phase stability enables the combined high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness attributed to these alloys.
